{
 "summary": "Fixes CMake package discovery when building depends packages by exporting CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH instead of CMAKE_MODULE_PATH in depends/funcs.mk. CMake reads CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH from the environment and uses it for config-mode package discovery, ensuring depends packages locate dependencies from the depends prefix rather than the host system.",
 "problem": "When building CMake-based depends packages such as native_libmultiprocess, CMake ignores CMAKE_MODULE_PATH from the environment and config-mode find_package() ignores it anyway. If a system version of a dependency like CapnProto is present on the host, CMake picks up the system headers and libraries instead of the ones installed in the depends prefix, causing build failures like version mismatch compilation errors.",
 "evidence": [
  "PR description documents a concrete build failure: \"This fixes a build failure in native_libmultiprocess where cmake would find the system (nix) CapnProto 1.2.0 instead of the depends-built CapnProto 1.4.0, resulting in a compile-time version mismatch error: #error 'Version mismatch between generated code and library headers.'\""
 ],

<category name="build" title="Build and CI">
## Covers

How the project is built, tested, and released: the CMake build system,
the depends system and its packages, Guix reproducible builds, CI
configuration and scripts, compiler and platform support, and the
tooling under contrib used for releases and development. Platform
labels (Windows, macOS) point here when the change is about building or
running on that platform rather than about a feature. The Build system
label is a strong prior.

Not build: source changes that happen to fix a compiler warning as a
side effect (they belong to their area).

## What matters here

Release integrity first: reproducibility of Guix builds, correctness of
dependency pinning and verification, and anything that could ship a
wrong binary. Then supported-platform breakage: a platform that fails
to build or run blocks users on it. Then CI reliability: flaky or
misleading jobs waste every contributor's time and hide real failures.
Then dependency transitions with deadlines (compiler or library minimum
versions, deprecations upstream). Then build time and contributor
friction.

Cosmetic CMake cleanups rank low unless they remove a recurring
breakage.
